chunks: From him, from Abu Abdillah al-Razi, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), who said:

I said to him: 'I have a female servant/slave with whom I have no marital relation nor a side (concubinage), and she is worth her price, but I had sworn an oath concerning her, saying: 'It is incumbent upon me that I never sell her.' And I have a need for her price, along with reducing expenses.' He said: 'God is with your word for him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on breaking an oath not to sell a slave when one needs the money for expenses?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) addresses a specific case of *yamin al-laghw* (oath of convenience) where the primary intent was not to bind oneself permanently but to serve a practical purpose. The Imam’s response, 'Filla bi-qawlika lahu' (God is with you regarding your word), indicates that breaking the oath to sell the slave for financial relief is permissible and divinely supported, reflecting the Shia juristic principle that oaths taken for temporary benefit do not strictly prohibit their reversal when the underlying need arises.
